questions.subtopic: 1A3 Organizational culture and ethics. Falling security near-miss reports
questions.question: A rail control center began counting each security near-miss report against the reporter's performance rating. Reports such as blocked phishing clicks then fell from 30 to 4 a quarter. What is the risk practitioner's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Stop using near-miss reports to rate individual staff
options.B: Make near-miss reporting mandatory under a new policy
options.C: Retrain control center staff on near-miss reporting
options.D: Set a near-miss reporting target in performance ratings

questions.key_concept: When reporting drops after reports start counting against staff, the cause is a disincentive; protecting reporters works where rules and training cannot.
questions.pre_read: Notice what changed just before the reports fell. Ask what that timing says about the cause.
questions.correct_explanation: The drop followed a change in how reports were used, so the cause is fear of consequences, not lack of knowledge. Leaders, as owners of the rating scheme, should end the reports' use in staff ratings, protecting people who speak up and restoring the reason to report. Retraining is the runner-up: staff who filed 30 reports a quarter already knew how, and training cannot outweigh a reason to stay quiet.

wrong_explanations.B: A mandate adds a rule but leaves the penalty in place, so staff still have a reason to hide near misses or report only harmless ones.
wrong_explanations.C: Training builds knowledge, and these staff reported freely before. While reports still count against them in ratings, training will not bring the numbers back.
wrong_explanations.D: A reporting target adds a count to the same ratings that penalize each report, inviting trivial reports while serious near misses stay hidden.

tips: Eliminate: B adds a rule while the penalty stays, and D sets a count in the same ratings that punish reporting.
Final two: A beats C because the cause is a disincentive, not a knowledge gap; protect reporters before teaching them again.
Exam cue: when reporting falls after a change in how reports are used, fix the incentive; culture follows what is rewarded or punished.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Glossary (risk culture); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RR-01 (organizational leadership is responsible and accountable for cybersecurity risk and fosters a culture that is risk-aware, ethical and continually improving)

questions.subtopic: 1A4 Policies and standards. Expired exceptions
questions.question: A telecom's exception register shows 30 exceptions to the patching standard. The exceptions expired up to a year ago, and the systems are still unpatched. What should the risk practitioner recommend as the BEST action?

options.A: Extend the 30 exceptions by a year in the register
options.B: Report the 30 lapsed exceptions to internal audit
options.C: Ask each risk owner to renew or close the exception
options.D: Have IT patch the 30 systems before the next quarter

questions.key_concept: An expired exception leaves risk carried with no current acceptance; the risk owner must decide again whether to renew it or restore compliance.
questions.pre_read: Notice what an expiry date is for. Ask what should happen to the risk when that date passes.
questions.correct_explanation: An expired exception means risk is being carried that nobody has currently accepted. Each risk owner must decide again: renew the exception on a fresh analysis, with approval at the right level, or close it and restore compliance. Having IT patch everything is the runner-up: patching may well be the result, but ordering it skips the owner's decision and may break systems that needed the exceptions.

wrong_explanations.A: A blanket extension in the register renews 30 risk acceptances without the owners' fresh analysis or decision; the practitioner recommends, but does not accept risk.
wrong_explanations.B: Internal audit gives independent assurance; it is not the route for management to resolve the owners' lapsed exceptions. The owners need to decide now.
wrong_explanations.D: Patching may be the right result, but ordering it skips the owners' decision and the reasons the exceptions were granted, such as systems that break when patched.

tips: Eliminate: A renews 30 risk acceptances in the register without the owners deciding, and B sends a management issue to the third line.
Final two: C beats D because an expired exception needs a fresh owner decision; patching may follow, but the owner chooses the response.
Exam cue: exceptions expire into a new decision by the risk owner, never into silent renewal or an order issued around the owner.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 ID.RA-07 (changes and exceptions are managed, assessed for risk impact, recorded and tracked); ISACA Glossary (risk owner)

questions.subtopic: 1A5 Business processes and resilience. Plan after an outsourcing change
questions.question: Six months ago, a manufacturer moved its order-to-ship warehousing to a logistics provider. But the manufacturer's continuity plan still relies on its old warehouse team. What should the risk practitioner recommend as the BEST approach?

options.A: Have the process owner update the plan for the new provider
options.B: Keep the plan until its next scheduled review
options.C: Propose a retest of order system failover with its owner
options.D: Rely on the provider's own continuity plan for the process

questions.key_concept: A process owner keeps its continuity plan current; after outsourcing, the plan is updated for the supplier, not replaced by the supplier's plan.
questions.pre_read: Notice what changed in the process and what the plan still assumes.
questions.correct_explanation: Continuity plans must follow the process they protect. Order-to-ship now depends on the logistics provider, so the plan's warehousing steps and contacts no longer work. The process owner, accountable for the process continuing, updates the plan for the provider's role, drawing on the provider's own arrangements. Relying on the provider's plan is the runner-up: it is useful input, but it protects the provider's service, not the manufacturer's process, and accountability stays with the manufacturer.

wrong_explanations.B: Waiting for the scheduled review leaves a plan that cannot work for months; plans are updated after major changes, not only on a cycle.
wrong_explanations.C: Failover testing checks the order system, which did not change; it says nothing about how warehousing continues through the provider.
wrong_explanations.D: The provider's plan is worth reviewing; however, it covers the provider's own service, and the manufacturer stays accountable for keeping its process running.

tips: Eliminate: B leaves an outdated plan in place until a scheduled review, and C tests a system that did not change.
Final two: A beats D because the manufacturer stays accountable for its process; the provider's plan is input to the owner's updated plan, not a replacement for it.
Exam cue: when a process changes, especially through outsourcing, its owner updates the continuity plan; a supplier's plan never replaces it.

questions.subtopic: 1B5 Risk frameworks, legal, regulatory and contractual requirements. New AI law
questions.question: A staffing agency plans to screen applicants with an AI model, and a law taking effect in nine months will class that use as high-risk. What is the risk practitioner's BEST course of action?

options.A: Ask the vendor to certify that the model meets the law
options.B: Assess the law's impact on the planned screening use
options.C: Wait for the regulator's guidance before assessing it
options.D: Recommend that the agency cancel the screening project

questions.key_concept: A new legal obligation is a source of risk: assess its impact on the planned use before its effective date, before relying on vendor assurance.
questions.pre_read: Notice how much time remains before the law applies. Ask what the agency must know before choosing any response.
questions.correct_explanation: A new obligation is a source of risk, and nine months is the time to understand it. Assessing the law's impact on the planned screening use shows which duties fall on the agency, such as oversight, testing or records, and who should own them. A vendor certificate is the runner-up: it can be useful evidence, but many duties fall on the system's user, and the agency cannot judge a certificate until it knows them.

wrong_explanations.A: A vendor's certificate covers the model, not how the agency will use it. The agency first needs to know its own duties as the user of a high-risk system.
wrong_explanations.C: Guidance may refine details, but waiting shortens the time left to meet duties that are already known. The impact assessment can start now.
wrong_explanations.D: Canceling is an avoidance response chosen before the risk is analyzed. The business decides once the impact and options are clear.

tips: Eliminate: C delays analysis the effective date makes pressing, and D chooses avoidance before the risk is known.
Final two: B beats A because the agency must know its own duties as the user before a vendor's certificate can show they are met.
Exam cue: a new law or rule triggers an impact assessment before its effective date; apply the principle, not a quoted clause.

questions.subtopic: 1B4 Risk appetite and risk tolerance. Appetite for AI uses
questions.question: An insurer's board has a low appetite for harm to policyholders, and units want generative AI in claims and customer service. Which of the following should the risk practitioner propose to BEST apply that appetite?

options.A: Allowed, review-needed and prohibited tiers of AI use
options.B: A minimum accuracy level for each AI model in use
options.C: A ban on customer-facing AI until regulators publish rules
options.D: CISO approval of each AI use case before launch

questions.key_concept: AI appetite becomes usable when it sorts uses into allowed, review-needed and prohibited tiers that owners can apply.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a business owner would need in hand when the next AI request arrives.
questions.correct_explanation: A broad appetite statement guides AI decisions once it says which uses fit. Tiers of allowed, review-needed and prohibited uses turn a low appetite for harm to policyholders into a rule owners can apply to each new use case, with closer review where harm is likelier. A minimum accuracy level is the runner-up: it is measurable, but accuracy is one property of a model and says nothing about which uses the insurer will accept.

wrong_explanations.B: Accuracy is one measure of a model, not an expression of appetite. A highly accurate model can still be used where harm is unacceptable.
wrong_explanations.C: Low appetite is not zero appetite. A ban chooses avoidance for every use before its risk is analyzed, including low-harm uses.
wrong_explanations.D: The CISO covers security, while decisions on harm to policyholders sit with business owners within the board's appetite. One technical approver does not express appetite.

tips: Eliminate: C treats low appetite as zero and bans every use, and D gives decisions on harm to policyholders to a security approver.
Final two: A beats B because tiers say which AI uses the insurer accepts; an accuracy level measures a model, not the insurer's appetite for harm.
Exam cue: to make appetite usable, look for statements that tell owners which activities fit, need extra review or are out of bounds.

questions.subtopic: 1A3 Organizational culture and ethics. Request for loss figures
questions.question: An industry peer group asks a bank's risk analyst for the bank's ransomware loss figures to build a sector benchmark. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Share the figures under the group's confidentiality promise
options.B: Share the figures once system names are removed
options.C: Decline to take part in the sector benchmark
options.D: Seek the bank's approval before sharing the figures

questions.key_concept: Information gained at work is released only with the organization's approval or under legal authority, so ask before sharing it.
questions.pre_read: Ask who has the right to decide what happens to the figures.
questions.correct_explanation: The ISACA Code of Professional Ethics asks members to keep information gained in their work confidential and not release it to inappropriate parties. The loss figures belong to the bank, so the first step is to seek approval from whoever can authorize their release, who may agree, set conditions or refuse. Declining is the runner-up: it protects the data, but it makes the bank's decision for it and may give up a useful benchmark.

wrong_explanations.A: A peer group's promise does not authorize release. The figures are the bank's information, and only the bank can decide who receives them.
wrong_explanations.B: Removing system names may reduce harm, but the loss figures are still the bank's confidential information, released without its approval.
wrong_explanations.C: Declining protects the data but decides for the bank, which may choose to share approved figures if the benchmark serves it.

tips: Eliminate: A treats an outsider's promise as permission, and B assumes that removing names makes the bank's data the analyst's to release.
Final two: D beats C because release is the bank's decision; the analyst seeks approval instead of refusing on the bank's behalf.
Exam cue: information gained at work stays confidential unless its owner, or the law, authorizes release; ask before sharing.

questions.subtopic: 1A6 Organizational asset management. Tools found at each count
questions.question: Each yearly asset count at an architecture firm finds cloud tools bought on staff expense cards. No one had listed them. What is the BEST fix for the risk practitioner to recommend?

options.A: Run the asset count each quarter instead of yearly
options.B: Record new tools at expense and purchase approval
options.C: Have IT scan the office network for new devices
options.D: Have IT block new cloud sign-ups from company laptops

questions.key_concept: Keep the inventory current by linking it to purchasing and change processes, not by more frequent clean-up counts.
questions.pre_read: Ask how these tools enter the firm without being recorded.
questions.correct_explanation: The tools are missed because they enter through expense claims, a route the inventory process does not watch, so the cause is a process gap. Recording each new tool when its expense or purchase is approved captures it, with an owner, as it arrives. A quarterly count is the runner-up: it finds the tools sooner, but it still relies on clean-up after the fact instead of recording them when they are bought.

wrong_explanations.A: A more frequent count shortens the gap but keeps the same cause. Tools still arrive unrecorded and are found only later.
wrong_explanations.C: Network scans find devices on the firm's network. Cloud subscriptions bought on cards run on the provider's systems and are easily missed.
wrong_explanations.D: Blocking sign-ups stops tools staff may need and is a control chosen before the risk is analyzed; it does not fix how tools are recorded.

tips: Eliminate: C looks for devices when the missing assets are cloud subscriptions, and D blocks tools instead of fixing how they are recorded.
Final two: B beats A because recording tools at purchase removes the cause; counting more often only finds them sooner.
Exam cue: when an inventory keeps missing the same kind of asset, fix the process that lets it in unrecorded, not how often it is counted.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 ID.AM-02 (inventories of software, services and systems managed by the organization are maintained); COBIT 2019 BAI09 (Managed Assets)

questions.subtopic: 1B5 Risk frameworks, legal, regulatory and contractual requirements. Supplier liability cap
questions.question: A hospital's imaging supplier kept a $50,000 liability cap. A breach of patient data at the supplier could cost $2,000,000. Procurement marked the risk as transferred. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Keep it marked transferred, with the cap noted
options.B: Record the loss the cap leaves as residual risk
options.C: Have the owner close the risk on contract signing
options.D: Ask the supplier to name an owner for the risk

questions.key_concept: A liability cap limits what a supplier repays; what the cap leaves stays with the enterprise as residual risk for its owner to weigh.
questions.pre_read: Compare the cap with the size of the possible loss.
questions.correct_explanation: A liability cap limits what the supplier repays, not what a breach would cost. With $50,000 recoverable against a possible $2,000,000 loss, most of the exposure, and every non-financial harm, stays with the hospital. Recorded as residual risk, the risk left after a response, it goes to its owner to weigh against appetite. Noting the cap beside a 'transferred' label is the runner-up: the label still tells leaders the risk has gone.

wrong_explanations.A: Noting the cap records the fact, but the 'transferred' label still tells leaders the hospital no longer carries a risk it mostly keeps.
wrong_explanations.C: Signing sets the terms; it does not remove the hospital's exposure to a breach of the patient data the supplier holds, so the owner has nothing to close.
wrong_explanations.D: The supplier can own its own controls, but the risk to the hospital's patients and objectives stays with a hospital owner.

tips: Eliminate: C has the owner treat signing as closing the risk, and D hands ownership of the hospital's risk to the supplier.
Final two: B beats A because the cap leaves most of the loss with the hospital; a 'transferred' label with a footnote still misstates who carries it.
Exam cue: contracts and caps shift some cost, not the accountability; record what stays with the enterprise as residual risk for its owner.

questions.subtopic: 1B2 Lines of defense. Second-line pay tied to the first line
questions.question: A trading firm's second-line risk analysts sit with its trading desk and challenge the desk's risk ratings, and their bonuses are paid from the desk's profits. What should concern the risk practitioner MOST?

options.A: Their challenge is less independent than internal audit's
options.B: The analysts sit with the desk instead of the risk team
options.C: Their pay rewards weak challenge of the desk's ratings
options.D: The desk, not the analysts, owns the risks behind the ratings

questions.key_concept: The second line needs objectivity: pay or reporting tied to the results of the unit it challenges weakens that challenge.
questions.pre_read: Separate what is normal in the lines model from what is not.
questions.correct_explanation: The second line needs objectivity, not audit-style separation, and pay drawn from the desk's profits rewards the analysts for rating the desk's risks low. That weakens the challenge the firm relies on. Lacking internal audit's independence is the runner-up: it sounds like the same problem, but the second line sits within management by design; what is wrong here is an incentive that pulls against its judgment.

wrong_explanations.A: The second line sits within management by design and need not match audit's independence; its need is objectivity, which the pay link undermines.
wrong_explanations.B: Embedding analysts with a desk is a common model that improves their insight; the pay link, not where they sit, threatens objectivity.
wrong_explanations.D: The first line owning the risks it runs is how the lines model works; the second line challenges those ratings and does not own them.

tips: Eliminate: B objects to embedding, a normal model, and D objects to the first line owning its risks, which is how the lines model works.
Final two: C beats A because the second line needs objectivity, not audit's independence; pay tied to the desk's profits undermines exactly that.
Exam cue: for the second line, look for conflicts that weaken challenge, such as pay or reporting tied to the unit it oversees.

questions.subtopic: 1B3 Risk profile. Reporting by risk category
questions.question: A retailer's board sets appetite for each risk category. The risk analyst's draft profile shows supplier risk 30% over its category appetite, but total exposure is within appetite. How should the analyst BEST report this?

options.A: As a total within the board's overall appetite
options.B: As a supplier variance within tolerance
options.C: As supplier excess above its category appetite
options.D: As one score averaged across the categories

questions.key_concept: Where the board sets appetite per category, each is reported against its own limit; headroom in one category does not offset an excess in another.
questions.pre_read: Note the level at which the board set its limits.
questions.correct_explanation: The board set an appetite per category, so each is a limit in its own right. Supplier risk is 30% over its limit whatever the others show: headroom elsewhere cannot absorb risk with its own causes and owners. The profile reports the excess for the board to decide on. Reporting the total as within appetite is the runner-up: the sum is accurate, but netting hides the excess the category limit exists to catch.

wrong_explanations.A: The total is accurate, which makes it tempting, but the board set limits per category; netting them presents one limit's excess as a position within appetite.
wrong_explanations.B: Tolerance is a deviation leaders set in advance; the stem sets none for supplier risk, so calling a 30% excess a variance within tolerance relabels it as allowed.
wrong_explanations.D: Averaging blends the supplier excess into the other categories, so what the board's category limit should catch drops out of view.

tips: Eliminate: B renames an excess as a tolerance no one set, and D averages the categories so it drops out of view.
Final two: C beats A because the board's limit is per category; a total within appetite does not cancel one category's excess over its own limit.
Exam cue: report each risk against the level where its limit was set; headroom in one category does not pay for an excess in another.

questions.subtopic: 1A1 Strategy, goals and objectives. Treatment outlasting its objective
questions.question: A telecom's board will close its fixed-line business in 18 months. But the fixed-line director's risk response plan still funds a two-year, $1,200,000 rebuild of the billing platform. What is the risk practitioner's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Report the rebuild to the board that decided the closure
options.B: Move the rebuild budget to the mobile business's risks
options.C: Ask the director to weigh the rebuild against the closure
options.D: Keep the rebuild going as the plan the director approved

questions.key_concept: When strategy ends or shortens an objective, the treatments planned for it go back to their owner to weigh against the new horizon.
questions.pre_read: Note what the plan was approved for and what has changed since.
questions.correct_explanation: The rebuild was planned to protect fixed-line billing, but that business closes in 18 months, before a two-year rebuild could finish. A treatment is worth its cost only while the objective it protects lasts, so the director, as owner, should weigh it again, perhaps against cheaper cover for the months left. Reporting to the board is the runner-up: the board set the strategy, but this treatment sits in the director's own plan.

wrong_explanations.A: The board decided the closure; revisiting a treatment inside the director's plan is the director's call, and the board sees the result in the profile.
wrong_explanations.B: Moving budget between businesses is a management decision; the practitioner brings options, and billing outages still need cover until the closure.
wrong_explanations.D: The plan was approved before the closure was decided; a rebuild finishing six months after the business closes may cost more than the risk it removes.

tips: Eliminate: B has the practitioner move a budget that management controls, and D keeps a plan whose objective ends before the rebuild is done.
Final two: C beats A because the rebuild sits in the director's plan; when strategy changes, the owner re-decides the treatment without the board deciding it.
Exam cue: when strategy shortens or ends an objective, the treatments planned for it go back to their owner to weigh against the new horizon.

questions.question: For three years, a grain cooperative sent recovery test results only to IT. So process owners, who set the targets, learned of missed targets only during real outages. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.B: Have IT retest each system until it meets its owner's target
options.C: Record this year's missed targets for their process owners
options.D: Report each recovery test's results to the process owners

questions.key_concept: Recovery test results go to the process owners who set the targets, so they can decide on any gap.
questions.pre_read: Notice who receives the results and for how long.
questions.correct_explanation: Recovery targets belong to the process owners, so test results are evidence they need to decide whether to fund a fix, accept a gap or revisit a target. Recording this year's misses is the runner-up: it helps now, but next year's results would still reach IT alone.

wrong_explanations.A: The board oversees appetite and major exposures, not individual test results; the process owners who set the targets are the ones who need them.
wrong_explanations.B: Retesting may follow, but IT would be choosing the response to gaps it does not own, and owners would still not see the results.
wrong_explanations.C: Recording this year's misses helps once, but results would keep going only to IT, so next year's gaps would again stay hidden.

tips: Eliminate: A sends test results past the owners to the board, and B has IT choose responses to gaps the process owners own.
Final two: D beats C because the cause is the reporting route; recording this year's misses helps once, but future results would still reach IT alone.

questions.subtopic: 1B3 Risk profile. Board question on a security program

options.B: The program owner's count of controls delivered on time
options.C: Risk owners' views on whether their own risks have fallen
options.D: Current ratings of the targeted risks beside last year's

questions.key_concept: A program's effect on exposure is shown by comparing the targeted risks' ratings over time, not by its spending or output.
questions.pre_read: Separate what the program did from what the board asked about.
questions.correct_explanation: Whether exposure fell is answered by the risk profile over time: the current ratings of the risks the program targeted, set beside last year's, show the change the board asked about. wrong_explanations.A: Spending against budget shows financial control of the program, not whether the risks it targeted are any lower.
wrong_explanations.B: Controls delivered on time measure the program's output; exposure falls only if those controls work against the risks they were meant to reduce.
wrong_explanations.C: Owners' impressions are opinions without the rating method behind them; the board's question needs ratings compared over time, not views.

tips: Eliminate: A reports the program's spending, not its effect on risk, and C collects owners' opinions in place of ratings made by the agreed method.

questions.subtopic: 1B1 Enterprise risk management (ERM). Impact bands after growth
questions.question: A textiles maker has quadrupled its revenue since setting its impact scale, and 70% of its risks now rate in the top band. What is the risk analyst's BEST basis for new bands?

options.A: The firm's current financial size and risk capacity
options.B: An even spread of today's risks across the five bands
options.C: The bands that a larger firm in the same sector uses
options.D: Each unit head's view of the rating their risks deserve

questions.key_concept: Impact bands show what a loss means to the enterprise now, so they follow its current size and capacity, not the spread of ratings.
questions.pre_read: Ask what an impact band is meant to tell a decision maker.
questions.correct_explanation: An impact band tells leaders how much a loss would hurt this enterprise, so its break points follow the firm's current size and the losses it can absorb. Bands set at a quarter of today's revenue overstate each loss's significance. An even spread of today's risks is the runner-up: it would separate them on a chart, but each band would then show a risk's rank, not what a loss would mean to the business.

wrong_explanations.B: Fitting bands to spread ratings evenly turns each band into a ranking, so a band no longer says how much a loss would hurt the firm.
wrong_explanations.C: A larger firm can absorb bigger losses, so its bands would understate what a given loss means to this textiles maker.
wrong_explanations.D: Bands set from each head's view of what their risks deserve vary by unit, so ratings could not be compared on one enterprise scale.

tips: Eliminate: C borrows a larger firm's bands, sized to its own losses, and D lets each unit head's opinion shape a scale that must be common to all.
Final two: A beats B because a band must say what a loss means to this firm; an even spread makes the bands a ranking instead.

options.C: A business owner for each schedule and budget risk
options.D: Risks that the system will not deliver the ridership gain

wrong_explanations.C: Business owners for delivery risks strengthen accountability, but the log would still miss the largest risk: a finished system that does not lift ridership.

questions.question: A rail freight operator's board set a six-hour tolerance for train-dispatch outages. The dispatch director owns that risk and wants the dispatch team held to a two-hour limit. What is the risk analyst's BEST response?

options.D: Report the two-hour limit to the board as a conflict

questions.subtopic: 1A4 Policies and standards. Cloud ban after an appetite change
questions.question: An office cleaning contractor's board has raised its technology risk appetite. But the contractor's IT standard still bans all cloud apps. What should the risk analyst recommend as BEST?

options.B: Refer the standard to its owner to match the new appetite
options.C: Lift the standard's ban on cloud apps across the firm
options.D: Publish the new cloud-app rules as an advisory guideline for teams

questions.key_concept: Policies and standards trace back to risk appetite; when the board changes its appetite, owners review the standards it affects and realign them.
questions.pre_read: Compare what the board will now accept with what the standard still requires.
questions.correct_explanation: Standards should keep risk within appetite without being stricter than it requires. options.B: Keep the builders accountable, with the business listed as Consulted

options.D: Share accountability between the team and the lending risk owner

questions.subtopic: 1A6 Organizational asset management. Assets valued by the revenue each earns
questions.question: A jewelry retailer's asset owners value IT assets by the revenue each earns directly, so the diamond-certificate records, which every diamond sale needs, rank last. Which of the following should concern the risk analyst MOST?

options.A: Owners rather than IT set the value of each asset
options.B: The values leave out the cost of reissuing the certificates
options.C: The values leave out sales that depend on the records
options.D: The values are not based on the assets' purchase prices

questions.key_concept: An asset is valued by what the business loses without it, including the sales and processes it enables, not only the revenue it earns itself.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the business could not do if each asset were lost, not only what it earns.
questions.correct_explanation: Valuing assets by the revenue each earns directly misses assets that other revenue depends on. Without the certificate records diamonds cannot be sold, so their loss would stop a major revenue stream, yet the ranking puts them last and risks to them would be underrated. Leaving out reissue cost is the runner-up: it is a real gap, but far smaller than the diamond sales the records make possible.

wrong_explanations.A: Owners are the right people to value their assets; the concern is the basis they used for the values, not who set them.
wrong_explanations.B: Reissue cost belongs in the value, but it is small beside the diamond sales that stop while the records are unavailable.
wrong_explanations.D: Purchase price is a weaker basis than business impact; it would rank the records low as well, since they cost little to create.

tips: Eliminate: A questions owners setting the values, which is their role, and D prefers purchase price, a weaker basis than business impact.
Final two: C beats B because the sales that stop without the records far outweigh the cost of reissuing them; both are gaps, one much larger.
Exam cue: value an asset by what the business loses without it, including the processes and sales it enables, not only the revenue it earns itself.

questions.subtopic: 1B1 Enterprise risk management (ERM). Framework kept by IT security
questions.question: A solar farm operator's IT security team maintains the approved enterprise risk framework. The team also rates its own security risks under that framework. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Add a chief risk officer review of IT security's framework changes
options.B: Split the framework into separate IT and business versions
options.C: Give internal audit the job of maintaining the framework
options.D: Move upkeep of the framework to the chief risk officer's function

questions.key_concept: The enterprise risk function, usually under the chief risk officer, keeps the enterprise risk framework; a team rated under its rules should not maintain them.
questions.pre_read: Note who keeps the framework and whose risks are rated under it.
questions.correct_explanation: An enterprise framework sets how every unit's risks are rated, so the function running enterprise risk management, usually under the chief risk officer, keeps it, and senior management approves changes. A team keeping rules it is itself rated under cannot apply them objectively, and its view is narrower than the enterprise's. A chief risk officer review of IT security's changes is the runner-up: it adds oversight, but the rules stay with the team they judge.

wrong_explanations.A: A review catches some changes, but IT security still keeps the rules its own risks are rated under, and the framework stays shaped by one team's view.
wrong_explanations.B: Separate IT and business versions recreate the silo that ERM removes; risks rated under different frameworks cannot be compared or combined.
wrong_explanations.C: Internal audit gives independent assurance over the framework; maintaining it would be a management duty that undermines that independence.

tips: Eliminate: B splits one framework into silos whose risks cannot be compared, and C gives internal audit a management duty it must stay independent of.
Final two: D beats A because oversight of changes leaves the rules with the team they are applied to; the enterprise risk function keeps them for every unit.
Exam cue: the enterprise risk function keeps the enterprise framework and senior management approves it; a team rated under the rules should not be their keeper.

questions.subtopic: 1A4 Policies and standards. A policy rule with no written steps
questions.question: A wealth manager's policy requires a call-back check before client-service staff change payment details, but no procedure says who calls or which number to use. Which of the following is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Task the client-service team with a written call-back procedure
options.B: Remind client-service staff of the call-back requirement in the policy
options.C: Write who calls and which number into the policy itself
options.D: Treat staff's current call-back methods as the procedure

questions.key_concept: A policy requirement is carried out through a procedure giving the steps, owned by the team that performs it; without one, practice varies.
questions.pre_read: Note what the stem says exists and what it says is missing.
questions.correct_explanation: The policy sets the requirement, but nothing tells staff how to meet it: who makes the call, and to which number. Procedures supply those steps and are owned by the team that performs them, so the client-service team writes one, approved by its manager, and the check becomes consistent. Reminding client-service staff of the requirement is the runner-up: it restates the rule, but leaves each person to decide how to carry it out.

wrong_explanations.B: Staff already know a call-back is required; a reminder repeats the rule without saying who calls or which number to use, so practice stays uneven.
wrong_explanations.C: A policy states intent and changes rarely; step-by-step call-back details belong in a procedure owned by the team that performs the check.
wrong_explanations.D: Staff's own methods were never defined or approved, so they may differ in ways that weaken the check; adopting them as they stand leaves the gap unexamined.

tips: Eliminate: C writes the call-back steps into the policy, which states intent, and D adopts whatever methods staff use, though nobody has defined how the check should run.
Final two: A beats B because no procedure says who calls or which number to use; a reminder restates the requirement but leaves those steps undefined.

questions.subtopic: 1B1 Enterprise risk management (ERM). AI use inventory kept outside ERM
questions.question: A paving contractor's innovation team keeps its inventory of 15 AI uses outside ERM. The uses include bid pricing. So their risks never reach the enterprise register. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Name the innovation team owner of the AI uses' risks
options.B: Build risk ratings into the team's own AI inventory
options.C: Rate the AI uses' risks within the enterprise register
options.D: Make the CIO owner of an AI section in the enterprise register

questions.key_concept: An AI use inventory lists what exists; each use's risks are rated in the enterprise register under business owners, so ERM compares and reports them.
questions.pre_read: Check where the AI uses' risks are rated and who sees them.
questions.correct_explanation: AI risks are enterprise risks: they belong in the enterprise register, rated like any other risk and owned by the managers whose processes use each tool, such as bid pricing, so leaders can compare, combine and report them against appetite. Making the CIO owner of an AI section is the runner-up: the risks reach the register, but under IT, though they fall on the business processes that use the tools.

wrong_explanations.A: The innovation team builds and runs the tools; the risks fall on the processes that use them, such as bid pricing, so ownership sits with those business managers.
wrong_explanations.B: Scoring the uses' risks in the team's own inventory still leaves them outside ERM, unowned by business managers and not compared with other risks or reported against appetite.
wrong_explanations.D: The entries reach the register, but under the CIO; AI uses such as bid pricing serve business processes, whose managers own the risks they create.

tips: Eliminate: A gives the risks to the team that builds the tools, and B rates them in the team's own inventory, which still sits outside ERM.
Final two: C beats D because AI uses such as bid pricing serve business processes; D brings the risks into the register but makes IT their owner.
Exam cue: when AI uses sit in a separate inventory, bring their risks into the enterprise register, owned by the managers whose processes use them, not by IT or the tools' builders.

questions.subtopic: 1A3 Organizational culture and ethics. Skipped checks in one region
questions.question: At a fiber network operator, one region's engineers skip cabinet-lock checks to meet output, with their regional manager's approval. Four regions on the same targets and training comply. What is the risk practitioner's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Run refresher training on cabinet-lock checks for the regional manager's engineers
options.B: Ask the lock policy's owner to tighten the cabinet-lock rules
options.C: Fit the region's cabinets with lock alarms the control owner monitors
options.D: Raise the manager's sign-off on skipped checks with the operations executive

questions.key_concept: When one unit breaks a rule that peers on the same targets and training follow, look to its manager's conduct, which leaders address.
questions.pre_read: Compare the region that skips the checks with the regions that comply.
questions.correct_explanation: Four regions on the same targets and training comply, so neither explains the gap; the regional manager's sign-off on skipped checks does. Culture changes when leaders hold managers to account, so the operations executive needs to deal with that sign-off. Fitting lock alarms for the control owner is the runner-up: they would catch open cabinets, but a manager who signs off on skipping stays in charge, teaching staff the rule is optional.

wrong_explanations.A: The manager's engineers had the same training as the four compliant regions, so knowledge is not the gap; they skip checks because their manager signs off on it.
wrong_explanations.B: The rule is not the problem: four regions meet it as written. A stricter rule leaves the manager's sign-off, the actual cause, in place.
wrong_explanations.C: Alarms would catch open cabinets, but the manager who signs off on skipping stays in charge, so the behavior, and the message that the rule is optional, continue.

tips: Eliminate: A retrains the manager's engineers, whose training matches four compliant regions, and B tightens a rule those regions already meet; neither touches the manager's sign-off.
Final two: D beats C because the comparison points to the regional manager; alarms catch the symptom, while accountability through leadership addresses the manager who signs off on skipping.
Exam cue: when one unit breaks a rule that peers on the same targets and training follow, look to that unit's leadership; the fix runs through accountability, not a new control.
